sm: Kyle Peterson hosts Potomac Watch with Wall Street Journal colleagues Colin Levy and Kim Strassel. They discuss Senate Republicans rushing to confirm conservative judges in the lame duck session, with only about seven weeks before Democrats take over. Colin says about a third of lower court judges are Trump appointees, but the Senate has confirmed only 57 judges so far this term. Three circuit court nominees and sixteen district court nominees are pending. They say vacancies are fewer than in the first term, because judges already took senior status or hesitate to retire, and vetting has been slower. They also note a dispute over a Texas district nominee, Elliot Geyser, whose blue slip Senator John Cornyn has not returned.

The panel continues on the Texas nominee. Cornyn prefers Steve Fehe, a longtime federal prosecutor, but Colin and Kim argue Geyser has solid conservative credentials, including clerking for Justice Alito and Judge Edith Jones and working at the Office of Legal Counsel. Kim says Trump and Cornyn are at odds after the primary, and with the Senate likely working only about five weeks, James Talarico would control the blue slip afterward and probably reject both. They also mention Arkansas senators Tom Cotton and John Boozman blocking Lee Rudofsky for the Eighth Circuit, with Cody Highland now nominated. Colin laments how polarized judicial nominations have become. The conversation then turns to Texas's governor-elect attacking the state's school choice program.

The hosts discuss the threat to school choice after Republican losses in the midterms. Kim says Texas's billion dollar program is less than one percent of public school spending, and that Democrats in Texas, Arizona and Wisconsin may try to cut or end existing programs. A state report found eighty-five thousand students from 895 districts confirmed they would use scholarships, eighty percent from lower income households and about a quarter with disabilities. Kyle notes that Virginia's governor, Abigail Spanberger, will pull out of the federal tax credit scholarship program, while Democratic governors in New York, New Mexico and Colorado opted in. An estimate from the American Federation for Children puts the lost money for Virginia at about 731 million dollars. Kim and Colin blame the teachers unions.
